cur:catacombs-priscilla-madonna-prophet.summary: On the vault of a tomb niche, painted over stucco, a seated woman holds a child at her breast, while a man in a tunic and pallium stands beside her, raising his hand and pointing upward towards a star painted above (outside this crop). The scene is read as the Virgin nursing the Christ Child, with a prophet – Balaam or Isaiah – foretelling his birth. It is counted among the oldest surviving images of Mary with Jesus, made in the earliest part of the Catacomb of Priscilla.
facts: The Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology dates this image of the Mother of God to 230–240 and identifies the pointing figure as the prophet Balaam, whose oracle speaks of a star rising out of Jacob.
On the same vault, beside the Virgin and Child, a Good Shepherd stands with his sheep among trees.

Wilpert, who published it in colour in 1903 (plates 21–22), believed it dated from the first half of the 2nd century and read the prophet as Isaiah; modern scholarship has lowered the date by about a century.

links.label: Catacomb of Priscilla (Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology)

cur:catacombs-priscilla-madonna-prophet.notes: Date refined from 'early 3rd century' (225) to the Pontifical Commission's 230–240; it remains in the 3rd century. The identification of the prophet (Balaam or Isaiah) is debated. A KU Leuven glass slide on Commons shows the Good Shepherd on the same vault (GD009644).

cur:manuscripts-etchmiadzin-gospels-ador.summary: Before a gabled architectural backdrop with a shell-shaped niche and drawn curtains, the Virgin sits enthroned in a deep purple mantle, holding the Christ Child in a mandorla-like oval before her; the Magi approach from both sides bearing gifts on veiled hands, with Joseph and an angel behind. The frontal, hieratic Child and Mother recall the icons of the early Byzantine world.
facts: The two leaves with the so-called 'Final Four Miniatures', dating to the late 6th or early 7th century, were bound into this Gospel book of 989.
The book of 989 was made at the monastery of Bgheno-Noravank in Syunik for Bishop Stepanos; its covers are two carved ivory plaques, probably Byzantine work of the 6th century.
cur:manuscripts-etchmiadzin-gospels-ador.notes: The exact folio (228 or 229, recto or verso) of this miniature is not given on the Commons file.

cur:monumental2-tokali-flight-into-egypt.summary: The Holy Family journeys from left to right in a frieze of haloed figures: the Virgin rides the donkey with the Christ Child, accompanied by Joseph and a young companion who leads the way. Drawn in soft reds and greens on a pale ground, the scene is part of the Infancy register of the Old Church vault, where the narrative closely follows apocryphal as well as canonical sources.
facts: The Old Church cycle draws on the Protevangelium (Gospel) of James as well as the canonical Gospels; it continues the Infancy story beyond the Flight into Egypt with the Murder of Zacharias and the Flight of Elizabeth.
Cappadocian painters often show a youth leading the donkey, identified in Byzantine tradition as James, Joseph's son from his first marriage.
cur:monumental2-tokali-flight-into-egypt.notes: The photographer identifies the leading figure as St James the brother of the Lord; this is consistent with Byzantine iconography but was not confirmed from an inscription.

Q116272858.summary: The Virgin, veiled and haloed, sits on a cushioned throne between columns, holding the Christ Child upright on her lap; the Child, with his own halo, raises his hand. Two winged angels lean over the canopy above, and a border of acanthus frames the scene. The plaque presents Christ as the incarnate Lord seated in his mother's lap, the throne of the Divine Wisdom.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to 850–875 and attributes it to northern France (accession 17.190.39, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
Its size (14.5 × 8.8 cm) and design match The Met's companion plaque of Christ enthroned with two apostles (17.190.41).
Q116272858.notes: Whether the two Met plaques were originally part of the same object was not verified.

met:473289.summary: Incised into a small cross of green steatite, the crucified Christ stands with arms outstretched and a halo behind his head, his body marked by ribbed lines, while the sun and moon appear above and small winged figures flank his arms. Letters are cut above his head. Simple and worn, this pocket-sized cross carried the image of the Crucifixion into everyday devotion in the Byzantine east.
facts: The Met records it as Byzantine, 11th century, made in Syria, and carved in steatite.
It passed through Ariadne Galleries, New York, to Miriam N. Rosen, who gave it to the Met in 2002.
met:473289.notes: Met 2002.483.4; 8.7 × 5.2 cm. Object type corrected from 'metalwork' to sculpture (stone). The incised letters were not read reliably from the photograph; the flanking figures look like angels but are worn.

walters:W.185.91V.summary: The body of Christ, still wearing the crown of thorns, is laid in a pink stone sarcophagus by two men, one at his head and one at his feet. Behind the tomb the Virgin in blue joins her hands in prayer, and John in red bows his head beside her, all set against a chequered gold ground. The quiet, tender scene closes the cycle of the Passion in this book of prayers.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
walters:W.185.91V.notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.
